comparison: Both strongly support the primary TSP findings (C7, C8, C22-C24, C31-C34, C38, C40-C41) with decisive Bayes factor evidence. Peer review R1 also encompasses additional TSP claims (C42-C46) that OpenEval addresses separately in R2, and includes C9 and C37 not in OpenEval R1. All reviewers describe evidence as 'compelling' and 'robust,' with full acceptance of the Bayesian methodology.

OpenEval R2 addresses TSP within OWM clades (C42-C45) as a distinct finding requiring functional validation. Peer R1 includes these claims within the broader TSP analysis without separate commentary, treating them as part of the comprehensive TSP evidence rather than highlighting their unexpected nature.

Both support gene conversion findings in MHC-A (C26) and lack of ancient TSP in non-classical genes (C28, C30). OpenEval R3 focuses specifically on C25-C26 regarding gene conversion, while peer R2 groups C26 with C28 and C30 as part of accepting negative findings. Peer review implicitly accepts through praise of 'appropriate methods and statistically rigorous analyses.'

Both support findings about MHC-E lacking ancient TSP (C28-C30). OpenEval R4 treats this as a distinct result with specific Bayes factor evidence, while peer R2 groups it with other negative findings as part of the comprehensive analysis without detailed commentary.

OpenEval R5 addresses the comparative finding that Class II genes show deeper TSP than Class I (C46). Peer R1 includes C46 within the broader TSP findings without specific commentary on this comparative pattern, accepting it as part of the comprehensive TSP analysis.

Both support evolutionary rate findings showing rapid evolution at peptide-binding sites (C47-C51, C58-C60). OpenEval R6 provides detailed analysis of statistical testing and quantitative percentages, while peer R3 accepts these findings through praise of the 'clever test for TSP complemented by positive selection tests and protein structures.'

Both support findings about MHC-E conservation (C52-C54). OpenEval R7 details the specific calculation that exons 2-3 contain only 45% of rapidly-evolving sites, while peer R3 accepts this as part of the comprehensive evolutionary rate characterization without specific commentary on MHC-E.

Both support findings about correlation between evolutionary rate and distance to peptide (C55-C57). OpenEval R8 details the regression analysis and statistical significance, while peer R3 accepts this through praise of integration with 'protein structures for a quite comprehensive study.'

Both rate C61-C63 as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval R9 supports the observation (C61) but notes the co-evolution mechanism (C63) is 'explicitly speculative and lacks direct experimental evidence.' Peer R6 similarly accepts the data but does not comment on the mechanistic interpretation, noting it 'remains in the realm of hypothesis rather than demonstrated finding.'

Both support regression analysis findings for Class II genes (C64-C66). OpenEval R10 details the contrast between genes with peptide-binding variation versus conserved DRA, while peer R3 accepts this as part of the comprehensive evolutionary rate characterization across MHC genes.

Both support disease association findings for Class I genes (C67-C68, C79, C84). OpenEval R11 details the regression analysis showing significant positive correlations, while peer R4 explicitly affirms that 'the fastest evolving codons are extremely enriched for autoimmune and infectious disease associations.'

Both support the finding that Class II genes lack significant disease association correlation (C69). OpenEval R12 notes the proposed explanation about slower evolution is reasonable, while peer R4 accepts this as part of the disease association analysis without specific commentary on the Class I/II difference.

Both support the contrast between classical and non-classical genes (C75-C77). OpenEval R13 emphasizes this provides 'strong evidence for the peptide-presentation-driven selection hypothesis,' while peer R3 accepts this through praise of the comprehensive approach to 'characterise evolutionary rates at individual codons.'

Both support TCR phenotype associations at rapidly-evolving positions (C78). OpenEval R14 notes the evidence connects evolutionary analysis with functional TCR data, while peer R4 accepts this as part of the broader disease association findings without separate commentary on TCR-specific associations.

Both support the integrative model (C80-C83) combining ancient TSP, rapid evolution, and disease associations. OpenEval R15 notes these are 'reasonable inferences from convergent evidence,' while peer R7 describes this as 'a synthesis and re-analysis of previous findings' that is 'extremely valuable and timely,' though noting 'discussion of the findings in the context of this literature is limited.'

Both support the diversity findings from 1000 Genomes Project (C16-C17). OpenEval R16 notes the 70-fold excess is quantitative and the inference of ancient balancing selection is reasonable, while peer R5 accepts this as background context consistent with established knowledge, with implicit acceptance through praise that the study 'makes the most of currently available genomic data.'

OpenEval R17 supports the contextual claim that MHC TSP is 'among the most ancient' examples of balancing selection (C70-C74), appropriately qualified with comparative literature. Peer R7 does not explicitly address these comparative contextual claims, though the acceptance of the integrative model implicitly supports this contextualization.

Both support the acknowledgment of data quality limitations (C85-C88). OpenEval R18 notes this represents 'responsible discussion of methodological constraints,' while peer R8 explicitly praises 'expansion of the discussion section on limitations' and confirms that 'false negative TSPs...as well as false positives...are well assessed and discussed.'

OpenEval R19 addresses established background knowledge (C1-C2, C11-C15) as 'accurate contextual statements rather than novel findings.' No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not separately evaluate background/contextual claims.

OpenEval R20 addresses established knowledge about MHC allelic diversity (C3-C4) supported by database citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not separately evaluate this background information.

OpenEval R21 addresses the rarity and significance of TSP as background context (C5-C6, C18-C21) through literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not separately evaluate this contextual framing.

OpenEval R22 addresses established knowledge about MHC-DR (C35-C37) and DRB TSP findings (C38-C39). Peer R1 includes C37-C38 within the broader TSP analysis without separate commentary on the DRA/DRB contrast or the companion paper reference (C39).

Peer R3 provides broad acceptance of evolutionary rate findings across multiple claim groups (C47-C77) that OpenEval addresses in separate results (R6-R8, R10, R13). Peer review treats these as an integrated comprehensive analysis rather than distinct findings, praising the 'clever test for TSP complemented by positive selection tests and protein structures.'

Peer R4 addresses disease associations broadly (C10, C67-C69, C78-C79, C84) that OpenEval separates into R11, R12, and R14. Peer review treats disease associations as a unified finding with explicit affirmation of enrichment at rapidly-evolving codons, while OpenEval distinguishes Class I versus Class II patterns and TCR associations.
